gloss: To move air onto something, or to make a fire or a strong feeling grow.
examples: Dry winds *fan* the wildfires every August.
She *fanned* herself with a folded magazine.
His speech was *fanning* the anger of the crowd.
contrast: Doubles the n before an ending: fanned, fanning.

gloss: To imagine something, especially to think of yourself as being something.
examples: He *fancies* himself a serious chef.
She *fancied* that someone was following her.
Don't go *fancying* yourself an expert after one weekend class.
contrast: The y becomes ie in fancies and fancied, but stays in fancying.

transitivity: both — transitive (he fantasized that he had won), intransitive (they fantasize about retiring)
gloss: To imagine pleasant things that are unlikely to happen.
examples: Kids often *fantasize* about being famous.
He *fantasized* that the letter would bring good news.
She spent the whole meeting *fantasizing* about her vacation.
contrast: American spelling is -ize; British books write fantasise.

gloss: To do well or badly in a particular situation.
examples: How did you *fare* on the final exam?
Small farms *fared* badly during the drought.
The team is *faring* better than anyone expected.
contrast: Sounds like fair, and looks like the noun fare (the money you pay for a ride).

gloss: To make or shape something by hand, often out of whatever is available.
examples: The villagers *fashion* tools out of scrap metal.
He *fashioned* a splint from two sticks and a belt.
She was *fashioning* a costume out of old curtains.

ru: становиться отцом, стать отцом; порождать, породить
gloss: To become the father of a child, or to create something entirely new.
examples: He *fathered* three children before he turned thirty.
Men who *father* children very young often finish school late.
*Fathering* a child at fifty-five surprised everyone who knew him.

gloss: To understand something puzzling after thinking hard about it.
examples: I can't *fathom* why she quit such a good job.
Nobody ever *fathomed* how the thieves got past the alarm.
The full scale of the damage still hasn't been *fathomed*.
contrast: Almost always negative: can't fathom, couldn't fathom.

gloss: To make someone very tired, or to weaken a material by stressing it again and again.
examples: Twelve-hour shifts *fatigue* even the youngest nurses.
The climb *fatigued* us far more than we expected.
Years of vibration had *fatigued* the metal until it cracked.
contrast: The silent -ue drops before -ing: fatigued but fatiguing.

gloss: To praise someone powerful far too much in order to win their favor.
examples: Junior staff *fawn* over the new director.
The waiters *fawned* on the celebrity all evening.
Reporters were *fawning* over him before he had said a word.
contrast: Takes over or on: fawn over the boss.

gloss: To disturb someone's calm or shake their confidence.
examples: Nothing seems to *faze* him.
The boos never *fazed* the kicker.
She was not *fazed* by the criticism.
contrast: A homophone of phase: faze means to unsettle, a phase is a stage.

gloss: To pretend to have a feeling, an illness or a reaction that you do not really have.
examples: Don't *feign* surprise — you knew about it already.
He *feigned* illness to get out of the test.
She listened, *feigning* interest in every word.
contrast: The g is silent: FAYN, exactly like the word fain.

gloss: To make a pretended move in one direction in order to mislead an opponent.
examples: Good boxers *feint* before they throw the real punch.
He *feinted* left and drove to the basket.
She kept *feinting* to pull the defender out of position.
contrast: Sounds exactly like faint (to pass out), but it is a different word.

gloss: To become infected, or, of a bad feeling or problem, to grow worse because nobody deals with it.
examples: Untreated cuts can *fester* quickly in hot weather.
Resentment *festered* for years before anyone spoke up.
The dispute has been *festering* since spring.

gloss: To decorate something by hanging chains of flowers, lights or ribbons on it.
examples: Volunteers *festoon* the square with lights every December.
They *festooned* the hall with paper flowers.
The porch was *festooned* with banners and streamers.
contrast: Usually festooned with something.

gloss: To tell a small, harmless lie.
examples: Kids *fib* about brushing their teeth.
He *fibbed* about his age on the application.
Stop *fibbing* and tell me what really happened.
contrast: Doubles the b: fibbed, fibbing.

gloss: To turn real events into a story by inventing parts of them.
examples: The movie *fictionalizes* the trial for dramatic effect.
He *fictionalized* his grandmother's escape in his first novel.
The series is a heavily *fictionalized* account of the war.
contrast: American spelling is -ize; British books write fictionalise.

gloss: To keep making small restless movements because you are bored or nervous.
examples: Try not to *fidget* during the interview.
The kids *fidgeted* through the whole ceremony.
He kept *fidgeting* with his sleeve while he waited.
contrast: One t in American spelling: fidgeted, fidgeting.

gloss: To think or conclude something after weighing it up.
examples: I *figure* we'll be there by six.
She *figured* the repair would cost a fortune.
*Figuring* she was already asleep, he let himself in quietly.
contrast: Different from the phrasal verb figure out, which means to solve or understand.

gloss: To get something by clever or slightly dishonest means.
examples: He can *finagle* a table at any restaurant in town.
She *finagled* an upgrade to first class.
They spent the afternoon *finagling* their way backstage.

gloss: To make small careful adjustments so that something works as well as possible.
examples: We still need to *fine-tune* the schedule.
They *fine-tuned* the engine the night before the race.
The team has been *fine-tuning* the app all week.
contrast: Written with a hyphen: fine-tune, fine-tuned.

gloss: To handle a difficult situation with skill, often by quietly getting around the hard part.
examples: A good manager can *finesse* a question like that.
She *finessed* the budget problem without firing anyone.
They are still *finessing* the wording of the deal.

gloss: To attack a building or vehicle with a bomb that sets it on fire.
examples: Extremists threatened to *firebomb* the warehouse.
Someone *firebombed* the campaign office overnight.
Three cars were *firebombed* on the same street last month.

gloss: Of a vehicle, to slide from side to side at the back because the rear wheels lose grip.
examples: Light trucks *fishtail* easily on wet roads.
The trailer *fishtailed* and nearly flipped.
He felt the car *fishtailing* on the ice and let off the gas.

gloss: To think about one thing so much that you cannot think about anything else.
examples: Don't *fixate* on one bad review.
He *fixated* on a single detail of her story.
The press keeps *fixating* on the candidate's age.
contrast: Takes on: fixate on something.

gloss: To produce a lot of small bubbles with a soft hissing sound.
examples: The tablet *fizzes* as soon as it hits the water.
The soda *fizzed* over the rim of the glass.
The champagne was still *fizzing* when we raised our glasses.
contrast: Adds -es in the third person: fizzes.

gloss: To begin with promise and then fail or fade away weakly.
examples: Most of these campaigns *fizzle* after a week.
The rally *fizzled* in the rain.
Their romance was already *fizzling* by June.
contrast: Often with out, as in the phrasal verb fizzle out, with the same meaning.

gloss: To astonish someone so much that they can hardly speak.
examples: The repair bill will *flabbergast* you.
The verdict *flabbergasted* everyone in the courtroom.
We were *flabbergasted* by how cheap the tickets were.
contrast: Most often passive: be flabbergasted by something.

transitivity: both — transitive (don't flail your arms), intransitive (he flailed in the water)
gloss: To wave your arms or legs about wildly, or to struggle with no control.
examples: Don't *flail* your arms — just float.
He *flailed* in the deep end until a lifeguard reached him.
The company has been *flailing* since the recall.

ru: располагаться по бокам; окружать с флангов
gloss: To be or move at the side of someone or something.
examples: Two stone lions *flank* the entrance.
Bodyguards *flanked* the senator as she left the building.
He arrived *flanked* by his lawyers.

gloss: To stop showing any activity or growth, whether a heartbeat on a monitor or a set of numbers.
examples: Wages *flatline* whenever hiring slows down.
The patient *flatlined* twice on the operating table.
Sales have been *flatlining* since January.

gloss: To charge someone far too much, or to cheat them out of their money.
examples: Some shops near the airport *fleece* tourists.
The contractor *fleeced* them for thousands of dollars.
Elderly customers were being *fleeced* by phone scammers.

transitivity: both — transitive (flick the switch), intransitive (her eyes flicked to the door)
gloss: To move something with a quick, light movement of a finger or wrist.
examples: *Flick* the switch on your way out.
She *flicked* a crumb off the table.
He was *flicking* water at his little brother.

ru: менять позицию на противоположную; идти на попятную
gloss: To switch to the opposite opinion or position, especially in politics.
examples: Candidates who *flip-flop* lose credibility fast.
The mayor *flip-flopped* on the tax within a week.
He's been *flip-flopping* about the job offer for days.
contrast: Doubles the p: flip-flopped, flip-flopping. The noun flip-flop is also a rubber sandal.

gloss: To move quickly and lightly from one place to another.
examples: Hummingbirds *flit* from flower to flower.
She *flitted* between three conversations at the party.
A shadow kept *flitting* across the wall.
contrast: Doubles the t: flitted, flitting.

gloss: To beat someone hard with a whip or a stick as a punishment.
examples: In those days the navy would *flog* deserters.
The prisoner was *flogged* in the public square.
Stop *flogging* that dead horse — the decision is final.
contrast: Doubles the g: flogged, flogging.

gloss: To drop down heavily, or, of a movie or product, to fail completely.
examples: After work I just *flop* onto the couch.
The movie *flopped* at the box office.
The fish was still *flopping* around in the bucket.
contrast: Doubles the p: flopped, flopping.

ru: чистить зубной нитью, почистить зубной нитью
transitivity: both — transitive (floss your teeth), intransitive (floss twice a day)
gloss: To clean between your teeth with a thin waxed thread.
examples: You should *floss* before you brush.
He *flossed* for the first time in a year.
*Flossing* takes less than a minute.

gloss: To struggle helplessly, either in water or in a difficult situation.
examples: New teachers often *flounder* in their first year.
He *floundered* through the interview and forgot half his answers.
The company has been *floundering* since the recall.
contrast: Not the same as founder: to flounder is to struggle, to founder is to sink or fail outright.

gloss: To break a rule or law openly and without shame.
examples: Drivers *flout* the speed limit on this stretch of road.
The company *flouted* safety rules for years.
They were fined for openly *flouting* the ban.
contrast: Not flaunt: you flout a rule but flaunt your wealth.

gloss: To do something clumsily or to make an embarrassing mistake.
examples: Don't *flub* the punch line this time.
He *flubbed* his lines in the very first scene.
She has already *flubbed* two easy shots.
contrast: Doubles the b: flubbed, flubbing.

gloss: To shake or pat something so that it becomes softer and fuller.
examples: *Fluff* the rice with a fork before serving.
She *fluffed* the pillows and straightened the quilt.
The bird sat on the wire *fluffing* its feathers.

gloss: To make someone so nervous and confused that they cannot think clearly.
examples: Big crowds *fluster* him.
The lawyer's question *flustered* the witness.
He got *flustered* and forgot his own address.
contrast: Usually passive: get flustered, be flustered.

gloss: To force something unwanted on someone.
examples: Don't *foist* your chores on your sister.
They *foisted* a useless warranty on every buyer.
New rules are being *foisted* on schools with no warning.
contrast: Takes on or upon: foist something on someone.

gloss: To deliberately stir up trouble, anger or unrest.
examples: Those broadcasts *foment* hatred between neighbors.
The article *fomented* days of protest.
He was accused of *fomenting* a rebellion.

gloss: To stroke or handle someone or something gently and lovingly.
examples: He would *fondle* the dog's ears while he read.
She *fondled* the fabric before deciding to buy it.
He sat *fondling* the old coin in his pocket.
contrast: With a person as the object it usually suggests unwanted sexual touching, so use it carefully.

gloss: To cross a river or stream at a shallow place, on foot or by vehicle.
examples: We had to *ford* the creek to reach the trailhead.
The wagons *forded* the river at dawn.
*Fording* the stream in spring can be dangerous.

gloss: To be an early sign of something that will happen later.
examples: The opening scene *foreshadows* the ending.
Falling orders *foreshadowed* the layoffs.
The storm was *foreshadowed* by an eerie stillness.

gloss: To warn someone about something before it happens.
examples: I should *forewarn* you — the main road is closed.
The city *forewarned* residents about the water shutoff.
We had been *forewarned* about the traffic.

gloss: Of a road, river or path, to divide into two branches.
examples: The trail *forks* just past the bridge.
The river *forked* around a small island.
Stay to the right after the road has *forked*.

gloss: To make an arrangement official by putting it into fixed, written form.
examples: We should *formalize* the agreement in writing.
The two schools *formalized* their partnership last year.
They are still *formalizing* the details of the merger.
contrast: American spelling is -ize; British books write formalise.

gloss: To work out a plan, policy or idea and put it into clear words.
examples: It takes weeks to *formulate* a good research question.
The committee *formulated* a new safety policy.
She is still *formulating* her answer.
